title: National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates: Using the Hays Salary Guide and Fair Work Pay Guides for Hourly to Annual Conversion
description: Compare the National Minimum Wage and award rates with the Hays Salary Guide FY25/26. Learn how to convert hourly to annual pay for a 38-hour week, including tax and super.
salarySummary: From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour for a 38-hour week, while award rates vary; the Hays Salary Guide provides typical salaries for professionals.

faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For a full-time employee on a 38-hour week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives a gross annual figure before tax and super. Remember that this assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

faqs.q: What is casual loading and how does it affect my pay?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra payment on top of your base hourly rate, typically 25% for most awards, to compensate for the lack of paid leave and other entitlements. For example, the National Minimum Wage casual rate from 1 July 2026 is $33.05 per hour (base $26.44 plus 25% loading). When using a calculator, you should enter your base hourly rate and then add the casual loading separately – never enter a rate that already includes loading.

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated on my pay?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at the super guarantee rate, which is 12% from 1 July 2026. It is not deducted from your salary. Your employer must pay this into your super fund, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For example, if your annual ordinary earnings are $60,000, your employer would contribute an extra $7,200 in super.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Hourly to Annual Pay in Australia

Whether you’re negotiating a job offer or checking your current wage, converting an hourly rate to an annual salary is a straightforward calculation. For a full-time employee working a standard 38-hour week, the formula is:

**Hourly rate × 38 hours × 52 weeks = gross annual income**

This gives you the pre-tax figure before superannuation is added on top. But the real picture depends on whether you’re paid the National Minimum Wage, an award rate, or a market salary from a recruiter survey like the **Hays Salary Guide**.

### The National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the Fair Work Ombudsman sets the National Minimum Wage at **$26.44 per hour** (or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours). This is the legal floor for award-free employees. Most workers, however, are covered by an industry or occupation award, which often has higher minimum rates. For example, the General Retail Industry Award might pay a Level 1 employee more than the national minimum. Award minimum wages increased by 4.75% from 1 July 2026, as confirmed in the [pay guides](/blog) on the Fair Work Ombudsman website.

If you’re a casual employee, you also receive a casual loading – usually 25% – on top of your base rate. For the National Minimum Wage, that means **$33.05 per hour** (including loading). Always enter your base rate into a calculator and tick the casual loading box separately; never type a rate that already includes loading.

### Using the Hays Salary Guide as a Reference

The **Hays Salary Guide** FY25/26 provides typical salary ranges for hundreds of roles across Australia. It’s a useful market benchmark, but it’s a recruiter survey, not an official wage instrument. The guide shows typical salaries (exclusive of super) for a 38-hour week, with a range around the typical figure. For example, a mid-level accountant might have a typical salary of $95,000, with a range of $85,000–$105,000. These figures can help you gauge what employers are offering, but they are not minimum entitlements. Always cross-check against the relevant award or enterprise agreement from the Fair Work Ombudsman.

When the Hays Salary Guide conflicts with official sources like the Fair Work Commission or the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the official sources take precedence. For instance, the ABS Average Weekly Earnings for full-time adult ordinary time employees was $2,083.70 per week in May 2026 – that’s about $108,352 per year. This is a national average, not a minimum.

### Calculating Your Fortnightly and Annual Pay

Once you have your hourly rate, you can work out your fortnightly pay by multiplying your weekly pay by two. For a full-time employee on the National Minimum Wage:

- Weekly: $26.44 × 38 = $1,004.90
- Fortnightly: $1,004.90 × 2 = $2,009.80
- Annual: $1,004.90 × 52 = $52,254.80 (gross)

If you’re on an award, your rate may be higher. For example, a hospitality award Level 2 employee might earn $27.50 per hour, giving an annual gross of $27.50 × 38 × 52 = $54,340.

### Tax and Super: What Comes Off and What Goes On

Your gross annual income is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office withholds income tax based on the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15c for each $1 over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: 30c for each $1 over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: 37c for each $1 over $135,000
- Over $190,000: 45c for each $1 over $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (based on 2025–26 single reduction thresholds). For a full-time worker on the National Minimum Wage ($52,254.80), the tax would be approximately $5,038 plus Medicare of $1,045, leaving a take-home of about $46,172. Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page for a more detailed estimate.

Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings by your employer at 12% (from 1 July 2026), up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. So for the same worker, the employer would contribute an extra $6,270.58 into super. This is not deducted from your salary – it’s additional remuneration.

### When to Use the Hays Salary Guide vs Fair Work Pay Guides

The **Hays Salary Guide** is best for understanding market rates for professional roles, especially when negotiating a salary. The Fair Work Ombudsman’s pay guides are the legal minimums you must be paid. If you’re covered by an award, the award rate is your floor – you can be paid more, but not less. The [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page explains the national floor, while the [pay guides](/blog) list all award rates.

### Important Caveats

This conversion assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. It also assumes you are an Australian resident claiming the tax-free threshold. If you have a HELP debt, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging, your take-home pay will differ. Always consult the Fair Work Ombudsman and the Australian Taxation Office for your specific situation.

In summary, the formula is simple: hourly × 38 × 52. But the right hourly rate depends on whether you’re on the National Minimum Wage, an award, or a market salary from the **Hays Salary Guide**. Use the official sources to check your minimum entitlements, and the guide to see what’s typical in your industry.
